dace967832e3bfa0: NEW DELHI: Russian president Vladimir Putin arrived in the Indian capital on Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.

Putin and Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese president Xi Jinping was also expected to meet him on the sidelines of the two-day meeting, according to Indian diplomatic sources.

Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India's external affairs state minister Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia's Ria Novosti news agency.

For China's Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE - three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement - the expansion of BRICS - today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
It will be Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.

"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
Indian foreign minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".
98b9191e948ffd49: EMPLOYEES come and go. It is one of the fundamental realities of working life.
People join organisations, develop their skills, build relationships, pursue ambitions and eventually, some decide it is time to move on.
They may resign for a better opportunity, a different challenge, personal reasons or simply because they feel ready for change.
That is their right.
An employment relationship is not a lifelong obligation. Employees should be free to resign when they believe it is the right decision for them.
Organisations cannot, and should not, expect people to remain simply because their departure creates inconvenience.
For business owners, however, an employee leaving can create a very real operational challenge.
This is particularly true for smaller organisations, where every individual may carry significant responsibility.
In a large organisation, the departure of one person can often be absorbed by a substantial team.
Responsibilities can be redistributed, temporary cover arranged and recruitment undertaken without bringing the entire operation to a standstill.
Smaller organisations rarely have that luxury.
When one key employee resigns, the consequences can be immediate. Workloads increase. Deadlines become harder to meet.
Other employees may have to take on unfamiliar responsibilities, while the owner may suddenly find themselves doing several jobs at once.
This can be frustrating, particularly when the departing employee is someone in whom the organisation has invested considerable time, training and trust.
Yet business owners must distinguish between disappointment and entitlement.
An employee may have been valuable, loyal and highly competent, but that does not mean the organisation owns their future.
The more productive question is not, "How do I stop people leaving?" but, "How do I build an organisation that can withstand people leaving?"
That requires a shift in thinking.

A resilient organisation does not depend excessively on any single individual. It develops systems, processes and knowledge that remain within the organisation even when the people who created them eventually move on.
Documentation is therefore not bureaucracy for its own sake.
Clear procedures, checklists, records and defined responsibilities ensure that important knowledge does not disappear when an employee walks out of the door.
Cross-training is equally important. When only one person knows how to perform a particular task, that person becomes a single point of failure.
Smaller organisations should encourage employees to understand one another's roles.
They do not necessarily need to become experts in everything, but they should have enough familiarity to provide continuity when a colleague is absent or leaves.
Business owners must also avoid building an organisation around personalities rather than roles.
A particular employee may be exceptionally capable, charismatic or trusted.
Nevertheless, the organisation should be structured so that the position can eventually be filled by someone else.
This is easier said than done, especially in small businesses where relationships are close and responsibilities overlap.
Owners naturally rely on people they know and trust, and that reliance can gradually become dependency.
Succession planning is therefore not something reserved for large corporations.
Even a small organisation can ask a simple question: If this person resigned tomorrow, what would we do?
The answer can reveal vulnerabilities that might otherwise remain invisible.
Retention, of course, still matters.
Employees are more likely to remain when they feel respected, fairly treated, properly compensated and able to develop.
They want to believe that their contribution matters and that their future has room to grow.
A business cannot prevent every resignation, but it can reduce unnecessary turnover by creating an environment in which good people have compelling reasons to stay.
Even an excellent workplace, however, will experience departures. People change. Circumstances change. Ambitions change.
The healthiest organisations accept this rather than treating every resignation as a betrayal.
Indeed, an employee leaving can sometimes be positive.
It can create opportunities for others to grow, bring new skills into the organisation and encourage the business to reconsider outdated practices.
The departure may even expose weaknesses that had remained hidden because a particular employee had been compensating for them.
Business owners should therefore develop a professional approach to resignation.
Thank the employee for their contribution, establish a sensible handover and capture as much institutional knowledge as possible.
There is little value in creating hostility during someone's final weeks. The person leaving today may become a client, supplier, business partner, colleague or advocate tomorrow.
At the same time, owners should resist the temptation to make one person's departure an organisational crisis.
A resignation should trigger a process, not panic.
The immediate priority is to identify what work must continue, what can temporarily be paused, what knowledge needs to be transferred and who can assume responsibility.
Recruitment can then take place thoughtfully rather than desperately. This is where leadership becomes particularly important.
Employees will inevitably come and go. What distinguishes resilient organisations is not their ability to prevent departures, but their ability to continue functioning when they occur.
That resilience comes from good systems, shared knowledge, sensible workforce planning, cross-training and a culture that values people without becoming dependent upon individuals.
There is also an important psychological lesson for business owners. Employees are not possessions.
They are people who choose to exchange their time, skills and expertise for employment.
That relationship exists by mutual consent.
An organisation that understands this is more likely to build genuine loyalty rather than obedience.
People who stay because they want to stay are far more valuable than people who remain because they feel trapped.
Ultimately, employee movement is not something business owners can eliminate. Nor should they try to.
The objective is to create an organisation capable of absorbing change.
When someone leaves, the business should certainly feel the loss. Good people matter. But that loss should not threaten the organisation's ability to function.
The strongest business is therefore not one where nobody ever resigns.
It is one where people can leave with dignity, new people can join with confidence, and the organisation continues moving forward regardless.

ca59711fda62cc6b: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's decades-old nuclear power ambition is returning to the table as rising electricity demand from data centres and volatile fossil fuel prices revive the case for a source of firm, low-carbon power.
But even if the government decides to proceed with nuclear power by 2030 or 2031, the country's first plant may only begin operating sometime between 2040 and 2046, an analyst said.

Malaysia has restarted its Phase 1 early-stage assessment under the International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) framework, with Malaysia Programme Office for Power Electricity Reform Corp (MyPOWER) tasked with coordinating the process.
The process requires the country to complete feasibility studies and establish a national position before making what the IAEA calls a "knowledgeable commitment" to a nuclear power programme.

MyPOWER, a company under the Energy Transition and Water Transformation Ministry, was established to drive electricity industry reforms before its mandate expanded to coordinate Malaysia's nuclear power programme.

CIMB Securities Sdn Bhd analyst Muhammad Afif Zulkaplly said the renewed assessment is timely as conversations over Malaysia establishing its own nuclear power plant have resurfaced among industry players.

He said the renewed interest comes as the conflict in the Middle East exposes vulnerabilities in the country's energy security while electricity demand accelerates on the back of data centre investments.
The assessment comes as the government steps up preparations for a possible nuclear power programme, although it has stressed that no decision has been made to adopt nuclear energy.

Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Datuk Chang Lih Kang said on Tuesday that Malaysia was already studying nuclear energy's potential role in its future energy mix, while undertaking preparatory work in technology, talent and regulation.

He said rising energy demand from semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, cloud computing and hyperscale data centres meant Malaysia needed to consider various options to meet its long-term power requirements.

"It does not mean that we have already made a decision but we need to be prepared so that our regulatory framework is ready, our talent is ready, and at the same time, we need to ensure the industry is also ready," Chang said.
The issue has taken on greater urgency as data centres consume a growing share of Malaysia's electricity.

Energy Commission data showed their share of overall electricity consumption hit a record 9.3 per cent in the second week of August, against an average of seven per cent so far this year, reports said.

Data centres could account for as much as 31 per cent of Peninsular Malaysia's electricity demand by 2035. At the same time, Malaysia will need another nine gigawatts of gas-fired capacity by 2032 as it progressively retires coal-fired plants.
Muhammad Afif said nuclear could provide firm and clean electricity while requiring less land than solar photovoltaic installations.

It could also reduce Malaysia's exposure to fluctuations in fossil fuel prices, particularly during geopolitical conflicts, while nuclear fuel's high energy density allows refuelling cycles to run for years.
"However, nuclear is not the cheapest or fastest new-build clean energy option, as it requires comprehensive long-term planning," he said in a note.
A DECISION BY 2030-2031?

The IAEA framework divides the development of a nuclear power programme into three phases covering 19 infrastructure issues, ranging from policy and regulation to ownership, financing, safeguards, workforce, emergency planning and waste management.

Phase 1 considers whether the country should proceed with nuclear power, while Phase 2 involves preparations for contracting and construction. Phase 3 covers the implementation of the first nuclear plant.
Assuming Malaysia completes the first phase, it could formally decide whether to adopt nuclear power by 2030 or 2031.

CIMB Securities estimated that another three to four years would then be needed for regulatory preparations, site assessments, vendor selection and commercial negotiations before construction or fabrication could begin.
This puts the possible commissioning of Malaysia's first nuclear plant between the early and mid-2040s, depending on the technology selected and any technological breakthrough, said Muhammad Afif.

The IAEA recently conducted a five-day workshop involving MyPOWER, the Malaysian Nuclear Agency, the Atomic Energy Department (Atom Malaysia) and Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB), among others, to help Malaysia project the manpower and skills required for a nuclear power programme.
TNB A LIKELY ANCHOR
One of the biggest questions is who would eventually own and operate Malaysia's first nuclear plant.
Muhammad Afif said national utility TNB is the most logical anchor operator because of its balance sheet and control of the electricity grid.
An independent power producer with nuclear experience could alternatively be awarded a concession to operate the plant.
Private-sector involvement during the initial stage is likely to be limited, the analyst said, except for TNB's potential role as the commercial delivery vehicle for the pioneering project.
TNB itself has begun preparing for such a possibility.
In its 2025 integrated annual report, the utility said it was exploring the opportunity to become a developer, owner and operator of nuclear power facilities over the longer term.
It said early investment in technical expertise, regulatory frameworks and partnerships with global nuclear agencies could establish the institutional capabilities required to operate nuclear assets.
CIMB Securities said Malaysia already has much of the institutional structure needed to begin its preparations.
MyPOWER is the country's nuclear energy programme implementing organisation, while Atom Malaysia would serve as the nuclear regulator.

The Malaysian Nuclear Agency would provide technical expertise and workforce training, while the Energy Commission would oversee electricity-market matters such as generation licensing, capacity procurement, grid connection and tariffs.
BIG REACTOR, SMR OR FLOATING PLANTS?
Malaysia has yet to decide what kind of nuclear technology it would use.

CIMB Securities said the country remains "technology agnostic", with conventional large-scale reactors, small modular reactors (SMRs) and floating nuclear power plants among the options that could be evaluated.
Conventional reactors of more than 1,000 megawatts offer economies of scale and have a proven operating record, but require substantial upfront capital and extensive site preparation.
SMRs, meanwhile, are designed to be factory assembled and transported to site, potentially reducing construction delays and allowing capacity to be added gradually.
"However, there are no proven commercially viable units yet that demonstrate replicable economics," Muhammad Afif said.
A third possibility is a floating nuclear power plant, where reactors are installed on a barge or platform offshore and connected to the coastal electricity grid.
Such a system could reduce land constraints and opposition to locating reactors near communities, although CIMB Securities said international maritime law presents potential complications.
Only one commercial floating nuclear power plant has been deployed domestically, in Russia.
WHO PAYS?
Beyond the technology, financing could prove to be one of the biggest hurdles.
Muhammad Afif highlighted nuclear projects in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkiye and Bangladesh as useful references for Malaysia.

At the UAE's Barakah plant, state-owned Emirates Nuclear Energy Company retained control while South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corp participated as the technology and construction partner and minority shareholder.
Turkiye took a different approach at Akkuyu, where Russia's Rosatom is responsible for financing, constructing, owning, operating and eventually decommissioning the plant.
Bangladesh retained state ownership of its Rooppur plant but relied heavily on Russian financing, leaving the country exposed to sovereign debt, foreign-exchange and project oversight risks.
In the case of Malaysia, Muhammad Afif said full foreign ownership is unlikely to be a viable option.

He said a structure similar to Barakah may be more appropriate, with TNB or another Malaysian company retaining control while an experienced foreign supplier provides minority equity, turnkey delivery and operating support.
"In our view, the final decision should focus on the allocation of liability for cost overruns, delays, operating underperformance, fuel and waste obligations, and long-term tariff risk," he said.
MAJOR QUESTIONS REMAIN
Despite the renewed momentum, CIMB Securities' assessment shows that some of the most consequential decisions remain unresolved.
Malaysia does not yet have a project cost, tariff model, site or outcome from a structured public consultation.

The owner and financing structure have not been decided, while arrangements for commercial spent-fuel disposal and funding for eventual waste management and plant decommissioning have yet to be established.
Regulation and emergency preparedness also remain under development.
Public acceptance could present another challenge.
CIMB Securities said negative perceptions remain one of nuclear power's main drawbacks, although acceptance appears to have improved in recent years.
The long lead time also means nuclear cannot solve Malaysia's immediate power needs.

Gas is expected to replace coal as the country's baseload source while Malaysia expands renewable generation, with nuclear potentially emerging as another source of firm low-carbon electricity over the longer term.
Malaysia plans to retire its last coal-fired power plants by 2044, while no additional gas-fired capacity is expected to come online this year or next, according to Energy Commission officials.

That leaves the country's nuclear assessment running alongside a more immediate challenge: securing enough reliable electricity for the next decade while demand from data centres and other industries continues to grow.

06ca795ec3b2d3b4: Now that the High Court judgment on the removal of liquid nicotine from the Poisons List has been delivered, and the government has withdrawn its appeal, it is tempting to tell the story with a few heroes, a few villains and one decisive moment where everything changed.

The reality is much less tidy, because tobacco control in Malaysia has never moved through one person, one organisation or one government. Almost every important step has depended on somebody moving the issue a little further before somebody else eventually inherits it.

I write this as the chairman of the Malaysian Council for Tobacco Control (MCTC), one of three organisations which brought the judicial review, the other two being Green Lung Malaysia and Voice of the Children.

The High Court held that the 2023 exemption of liquid and gel nicotine used in electronic cigarettes and vaping devices from the Poisons List was irrational, made without proper and effective consultation with the Poisons Board, and failed to adequately protect public health and Malaysia’s commitments to prevent and reduce nicotine addiction – but the road to that judgment began long before this controversy.

What is less visible is what it took to bring the challenge, because there was no commercial interest behind us, no financial return waiting at the end, and no guarantee that after the expenditure of time, money and professional energy, we would succeed.

Civil society bore the cost, individuals contributed personally, lawyers contributed their time and expertise, and there were periods when support around us was much thinner than it appears in retrospect, including pressure not to proceed and genuine concern among some involved about what taking a government decision to court might mean professionally.

We did not make the decision lightly, and before litigation there were repeated attempts at engagement. Eventually, however, we believed the matter required legal determination. That experience is important to remember now, not because it makes civil society heroic or the government the villain, but because public interest action often takes place when the outcome is uncertain, the costs are real, and those involved have very little to gain personally from continuing.
The longer history matters even more, because Malaysian tobacco control did not begin in 2023 and did not begin when vaping entered the national conversation.

Dr Lekhraj Rampal has been part of this struggle for more than four decades, while many others have carried institutional memory from one tobacco control battle to the next, remaining engaged through years when legislation stalled, public attention moved elsewhere and advocacy frequently produced more disappointment than visible progress.
The political history is similarly complicated, and public policy cannot easily be divided into people who were simply right and people who were simply wrong.
When Khairy Jamaluddin was health minister, he took comprehensive tobacco control legislation and the generational endgame further than they had travelled before.

Dr Zaliha Mustafa, although she made the nicotine exemption which we later challenged, was also the minister who brought the Control of Smoking Products for Public Health Bill back onto the floor of Parliament. She carried the remaining legislation forward when the generational endgame could no longer survive the political and legal process.

Then Dzulkefly Ahmad inherited the legislation, its implementation, the litigation and, ultimately, the decision on whether the government should continue appealing the High Court judgment. His contribution forms part of the same continuum.

One minister moves an idea forward, another may make a decision we profoundly disagree with while advancing another part of policy, and another inherits the unfinished work, while civil servants, MPs, doctors, pharmacists, academics, lawyers and civil society organisations continue pushing from different directions.

The legal challenge required another form of contribution, because public health conviction alone does not make a judicial review. Our lawyers helped translate our concern into questions of law, evidence, administrative power and proper decision-making which a court could determine. This is why I do not believe the judgment should be anybody's personal trophy, because public health victories become stronger when people believe they belong collectively to society rather than to one NGO, one minister, one lawyer or one generation of advocates.

Malaysia's experience over more than three decades has shown that public health rarely gives us one great final victory. Instead, it offers progress accumulated over time, a law moved forward by one person and carried further by another, a decision challenged, a judgment delivered, a government eventually changing course, and another generation inheriting what remains unfinished.

For me, there is also something particularly personal in how this chapter ends. Before I became an advocate, before I became involved in health systems or tobacco control, I was and remain a physician, and I am proud and grateful that this effort, in whatever small way, may have contributed.

I have been able not only to heal where I can, but also to prevent harm, and in doing so, to try to live up to one of the oldest and most revered principles of our profession, primum non nocere – first, do no harm.

861c7b1a3932560a: PETALING JAYA: Hukuman sebat terhadap scammer mungkin memberi kesan pencegahan, tetapi tidak cukup untuk menumpaskan sindiket penipuan dalam talian yang kompleks dan beroperasi merentas sempadan, kata pakar keselamatan siber.

Presiden Persatuan Pengguna Siber Malaysia (MCCA), Siraj Jalil, berkata keberkesanan hukuman lebih berat bergantung kepada keupayaan pihak berkuasa memastikan pelaku benar-benar ditangkap, didakwa dan dihukum.
Katanya, kebanyakan tangkapan di Malaysia membabitkan pemilik akaun keldai yang bertindak sebagai perantara bawahan, sedangkan dalang utama sindiket boleh terus beroperasi dari luar negara.
“Perantara bawahan ini mudah diganti dan dieksploitasi selagi aliran keuntungan haram dapat dialihkan dengan pantas.
“Mengenakan hukuman fizikal ke atas keldai akaun tidak akan melumpuhkan sindiket,” katanya kepada FMT.

Beliau mengulas kenyataan Ketua Polis Negara Mohd Khalid Ismail yang mencadangkan kerajaan meminda undang-undang lapuk dan mengenakan hukuman lebih berat, termasuk sebat, terhadap penjenayah penipuan dalam talian.
Mengulas lanjut, Siraj berkata usaha pencegahan perlu menumpukan tindakan memutuskan laluan pengubahan wang haram serta menutup ruang teknologi yang mudah dieksploitasi penjenayah.

Beliau berkata, sektor perbankan menunjukkan kemajuan, termasuk menerusi langkah Bank Negara Malaysia memperkukuh keselamatan digital dan pengesahan transaksi, namun tahap keselamatan sektor telekomunikasi masih perlu dipertingkatkan secara agresif.
Katanya, kelemahan itu termasuk lambakan kad SIM berdaftar palsu di platform e-dagang, penggunaan stesen pangkalan palsu atau fake BTS/IMSI-catcher serta manipulasi gerbang mesej.
“Perkhidmatan telekomunikasi masih terlalu rapuh dan menjadi instrumen utama eksploitasi penjenayah siber,” katanya yang turut mencadangkan pemerkasaan Pusat Respons Scam Kebangsaan (NSRC).
Sementara itu, aktivis keselamatan siber Aaron Mokhtar berkata hukuman sebat bukan langkah yang salah dari sudut simbolik, tetapi tidak memadai sebagai strategi utama membendung jenayah siber.
"Lebih berkesan dengan menyasarkan rangkaian kewangan dan akaun keldai yang digunakan untuk memindahkan wang hasil penipuan.
"Usaha itu perlu disokong dengan pengukuhan kerangka undang-undang dan penguatkuasaan siber, selain kerjasama antarabangsa serta diplomatik," katanya.
Berbeza dengan Siraj dan Aaron, pakar keselamatan siber Fong Choong Fook menyokong hukuman sebat dengan alasan sindiket penipuan tidak lagi gentar terhadap hukuman berbentuk kewangan.

“Hukuman yang lebih berat akan menjadi faktor pencegah yang jauh lebih kuat. Penipu pada masa kini tidak begitu bimbang tentang pembayaran ganti rugi kewangan kerana mereka mampu membayar ganti rugi tersebut,” katanya.
6384ef9e6b503dcc: The Lau King Howe Hospital Memorial Museum is a tribute to a cherished former hospital and the respected philanthropist behind its establishment.
Established in 1936, the Lau King Howe Hospital was Sibu’s first modern medical facility. It remained the region’s only one until 1994, when a new General Hospital opened in town.
It, therefore, played an important role in the lives of generations of local residents for close to six decades.

Lau King Howe was born the son of a pastor in 1869, in China’s Fujian province. After studying at the Methodist Anglo-Chinese College in Foochow, he trained as a teacher in the Philippines and later became principal of the Philippines Chinese School.
He returned to China in 1914 and, after a period in government service, went into business in Shanghai.
In 1916, at age 47, Lau moved to Sibu in search of better opportunities. He established a rubber plantation and went on to make his fortune there.

Towards the end of his life, concerned by the limited medical facilities available in Sibu, he proposed to the Rajah Brooke government in 1930 that a new hospital be built, with the cost shared between himself and the government.
Rather than leave all his wealth to his sons, whom he feared might squander it, Lau believed some of it would be better used to build a hospital for the community.
Construction began in 1931. Alas, Lau did not live to see the hospital completed, though it was named in his honour.

After the General Hospital opened in Sibu in 1994, Lau King Howe Hospital closed. Much of the original complex was subsequently demolished, but the outpatient clinic, pharmacy and emergency departments were preserved and converted into the memorial museum.
The exhibits offer a glimpse into the wide range of services once provided by the hospital, from maternity care and dentistry to pharmacy and emergency treatment.
One photograph shows nurses caring for Siamese twins, while another display traces the changing styles of nurses’ uniforms over the decades.
Among the smaller details is an ornate Sarawak brass belt buckle once worn as part of a nurse’s uniform.
The pharmacy section is particularly interesting, with stories about the once-familiar “KK” tablet (paracetamol), as well as the practical ways medicines were dispensed in earlier decades.
Liquid medication, for example, was sometimes given out in repurposed ketchup or beer bottles!
Visitors can also learn how iodine was added to Sibu’s salt supply in an effort to reduce cases of goitre.

Together, these small objects and stories offer a fascinating glimpse into an era when medical care looked very different, while preserving the memory of an institution that served Sibu for almost 60 years.
The Lau King Howe Hospital Memorial Museum may be small, but it packs in plenty of local history and intriguing details about healthcare in Sarawak.
It is air-conditioned, admission is free, and donations are welcome.
Lau King Howe Hospital Memorial Museum Jalan Lau King Howe, 96000 Sibu, Sarawak
